**Ideas to find new inspiration:**

- **Rework your 30-day challenge with a constraint.** Instead of “paint every day,” try “one flower study a day,” “palette-knife only,” “limited 3-color palette,” or “15-minute studies.” Constraints often make the work feel fresher.
- **Build a small themed series.** Since you’ve been thinking about impermanence, paint the same flower or object at different stages—bud, full bloom, wilting, dried—or paint the same subject under different light. This gives you a direction without requiring a huge idea.
- **Combine your interests in flowers and texture.** Do one realistic flower study, then a purely palette-knife/impasto version of the same flower. Compare what each approach teaches you.
- **Take your own reference photos.** Use natural light, multiple angles, and close-up detail shots instead of relying only on Instagram. Photograph flowers, fabric, shadows, or ordinary objects around your apartment.
- **Join an art class, group, or online challenge.** This fits your earlier interest in reconnecting with people and gives you accountability and fresh feedback.
- **Change your studio input.** Rotate what’s on your inspiration wall, add a plant or object with interesting texture, play different music, or visit a garden/gallery/market with a sketchbook—not to finish a painting, just to collect ideas.
- **Lower the stakes.** Make small, disposable studies or “ugly” experiments. Sometimes being stuck comes from expecting each painting to be a finished piece.

If you want one starting point: **paint a short series of the same flower using three different approaches—realistic, palette-knife textured, and abstract color study.** That uses what you already enjoy and gives you a clear container to experiment in.
